title: Syndrome-Resolved Decoding of Qubit Readout Errors
authors: Han Zheng, Vladimir Pešić, Nikolay Gusarov, Andrea Lizzit, Taketo Imaizumi, Chulwoo Ahn, Marco Nicolas Mueller, Raymond Mencia, Edoardo Charbon, Vladimir E. Manucharyan
abstract: Readout errors in superconducting qubits include incorrect state assignment, bit flips within the computational subspace, and leakage to non-computational states. These errors require different mitigation strategies, yet conventional measurement fidelity and repeatability metrics do not resolve their individual contributions. Previous repeated-readout studies have shown that temporal correlations reveal additional information about readout errors. Here we introduce the Readout Error Decoder (RED), which converts repeated thresholded binary records into a channel-resolved error budget. Controlled error injections validate the channel-specific response of the decoder. We demonstrate RED on both fluxonium and transmon qubits and across distinct leakage-lifetime regimes. RED identifies the error channels limiting readout performance without requiring dedicated discrimination of non-computational states, providing a basis for targeted readout optimization across different qubit modalities.
summary: This work introduces the Readout Error Decoder (RED), a novel technique to diagnose and quantify individual readout error channels—such as bit-flips, assignment errors, and leakage—in superconducting qubits. By analyzing temporal correlations across multiple measurements, RED bypasses the need for perfect state discrimination. This provides a vital, targeted diagnostic tool for optimizing qubit readout fidelity across various superconducting platforms.
main_problem: Readout errors in superconducting qubits (assignment, bit-flips, leakage) are difficult to quantify because conventional metrics cannot resolve their individual contributions.
main_result: The Readout Error Decoder (RED) successfully separates and quantifies these distinct error channels using temporal correlations from repeated measurements, even without dedicated state discrimination.
method: RED converts repeated, thresholded binary readout records into a channel-resolved error budget by analyzing syndrome patterns derived from correlations between successive measurements.
model_or_system: The study uses superconducting qubits, specifically fluxonium and transmon architectures, as the physical platform for testing the error decoding protocol.
key_observables: Error rates for assignment error, bit-flip error, and leakage; coherence times ($T_q$); and syndrome patterns ($S1, S2, S3+$).
important_parameters: Readout duration ($t_{RO}$); leakage lifetimes ($	au_{leak}$); and gate sequences ($I, X, X-	au-X$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the error patterns leave distinct, measurable signatures in the temporal correlation records, allowing for channel separation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the RED protocol overview, validation via controlled error injection, and the dependence of error rates (assignment/bit-flip) on readout duration for different qubit types.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the RED protocol, validates it using controlled error injections on multiple superconducting qubit types, quantifies the separated error rates across different leakage regimes, and compares derived coherence times to independent measurements.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful, general diagnostic tool for characterizing measurement-induced decoherence in solid-state qubits, which is crucial for scaling up quantum processors.

(b) The two ways the qubit state can change during the readout: a flip inside the computational subspace, |g⟩↔|e⟩, and leakage to the non-computational state |l⟩. (c) The RED sequence and its analysis. Readouts are interleaved with a fixed gate G ∈{I, X, X-τ-X}, which gives the gate record G, the measured record m, and the correlation record c. FIG. 2. Controlled error-injection validation of RED. (a) Bit flips are injected by a π01 pulse applied with proba- bility Pb on I sequences prepared in |g⟩and |e⟩: the extracted bit-flip channel tracks Pb with near-unit slope on both prepa- rations, while the assignment channel remains nearly flat. (b) Leakage is injected by a π12 pulse applied with probability Pf starting from |e⟩. The extracted leakage error from the X-τ- X sequence increases linearly with Pf with a fitted slope of 0.887, while the raw S1 rate of the I reference remains nearly constant. Data are taken on fluxonium qubits.

A long-lived leakage persists over many readout cycles and breaks a run of correlations; a short-lived leakage returns within one cycle and breaks only one correlation at most. (b) Long-lived-leakage probe: repeated readouts with an inter-readout X gate. (c) Transmon data, S3+ versus readout duration.
